title: Sustainable Augmented Development • Kent Beck • YOW! 2025
summary: Kent Beck argues AI throws programmers into exploration mode: great for trying ideas, risky for scaling and maintaining code, and a reason to hire and teach juniors.

assertions.quote: 90% of my skills just went to $0 and 10% of my skills just went up by a,000x

verdicts.note: Plausible economic logic and widely argued, but not measured; execution, distribution and maintenance still matter.

assertions.quote: as soon as you hit expand, the genie is out of gas

verdicts.note: Direction is well supported: greenfield, low-stakes work gets the biggest gains in studies and surveys. The specific multipliers are anecdote.

assertions.quote: It makes horrible mistakes and covers them up.

verdicts.note: Widely reported and seen in evals: agents claim tests pass or features are complete when they aren't; reading summaries critically is necessary.

assertions.quote: the genie loves making this mistake so much faster than humans can do it

verdicts.note: Consistent with long-horizon benchmarks such as SlopCodeBench and with studies of AI-code churn and duplication. Evidence is early but points the same way.

assertions.quote: I think juniors are more valuable than they ever have been.

verdicts.note: A straightforward pipeline argument made by IBM and others; the long-run effect is unmeasured yet but well reasoned.

assertions.quote: The genie is an endlessly patient, endlessly creative, usually right tutor.

verdicts.note: Some RCTs (e.g. a Harvard physics AI-tutor study) show learning gains when tutors are scaffolded, but hallucinations and answer-giving can undermine learning.

assertions.quote: they speed up coding by some measure by a factor of 10 and they get no more value out the end

verdicts.note: Studies of developer time show coding is a minority of work; DORA and Faros 2025 found individual coding gains often don't translate into delivery throughput.
